```{r}
#| echo: False
#The following code was not written by myself but taken from my data science class. Credit to Scott Appleby.
required_packages <-function(...) { 
  libs<-unlist(list(...)) 
  req<-suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(unlist(lapply(libs,require,character.only=TRUE)))) 
  need<-libs[req==FALSE] 
  if(length(need)>0){ 
    install.packages(need, repos = "http://cran.us.r-project.org") 
    lapply(need, library, character.only=TRUE) 
  }
  else{message("No packages required installation.")} 
}

required_packages("tidyverse", "readxl", "lme4", "lmerTest", "emmeans", "car")
```


```{r load}
Stat_All <- read_xlsx("Prelim Stat All 2026.xlsx")
```


```{r mean, echo=FALSE}

Stat_HourlyAvgsLong <- Stat_All %>%
  mutate(Time = hms(format(DateTime, "%H:%M:%S"))) %>% 
  #filter(Time >= hms("20:00:00") | Time <= hms("06:30:00")) %>%
  #For nighttime temperature statistics, includeline above instead of line below
  #filter(Time <= hms("20:00:00") & Time >= hms("06:30:00")) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Ambient, Sun, Shade), names_to = "Location", values_to = "Temperature") %>% 
  group_by(Time, Site, Campus, Month, Location) %>%
  summarize(
        mean = mean(Temperature, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd   = sd(Temperature, na.rm = TRUE),
        n    = sum(!is.na(Temperature)),
        se   = sd(Temperature, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(Temperature))),
        cv   = sd(Temperature, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(Temperature, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
        .groups = "drop_last") %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  filter(n >= 3)

Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer <- Stat_HourlyAvgsLong %>%
  filter(!is.na(mean)) %>% 
  mutate(Time = as.numeric(Time)/3600, 
         Site = as.factor(Site), 
         Campus = as.factor(Campus))
```

```{r mean, echo=FALSE}
#sun mean & cv
HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunMean <- lmer(mean~Site*Month+poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Sun"))
HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunCV <- lmer(cv~Site*Month+poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Sun"))
#shade mean & cv
HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeMean <- lmer(mean~Site*Month+poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Shade"))
HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeCV <- lmer(cv~Site*Month+poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Shade"))
#ambient mean & cv
HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbMean <- lmer(mean~Site*Month+poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Ambient",
                                      !Campus == "CSUSM"))
HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbCV <- lmer(cv~Site*Month+poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Ambient",
                                      !Campus == "CSUSM"))
```

## Model Diagnostics: Model Collinearity & Overall Fit

We check to see if models display collinearity, meaning that terms should likely not coexist within the model.

```{r}
vif(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunMean)
vif(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunCV)
vif(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeMean)
vif(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeCV)
vif(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbMean)
vif(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbCV)

AIC(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunMean)
AIC(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunCV)
AIC(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeMean)
AIC(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeCV)
AIC(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbMean)
AIC(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbCV)
```

It appears that the site and month interaction may not need to be included in the model since the main effects are highly multicollinear with the interaction. This is not something we can fix with centering since they are both categorical variables. We will opt to exclude the interaction from here on out.

## Model Diagnostics: Residual Plots

```{r}
plot(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunMean, main = "Sun Mean Model")
plot(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunCV, main = "Sun CV Model")
plot(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeMean, main = "Shade Mean Model")
plot(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeCV, main = "Shade CV Model")
plot(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbMean, main = "Ambient Mean Model")
plot(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbCV, main = "Ambient CV Model")

qqnorm(resid(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunMean), main = "Sun Mean Model")
qqnorm(resid(HourlyAvgs_lmer_SunCV), main = "Sun CV Model")
qqnorm(resid(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeMean), main = "Shade Mean Model")
qqnorm(resid(HourlyAvgs_lmer_ShadeCV), main = "Shade CV Model")
qqnorm(resid(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbMean), main = "Ambient Mean Model")
qqnorm(resid(HourlyAvgs_lmer_AmbCV), main = "Ambient CV Model")
```

This is indicative that some of the model assumptions (LINE: Linearity, Independence, Normally Distributed Residuals, Equal Variance) are violated. Namely, in the Sun Mean model, Sun CV model, the Shade Mean model, the Shade CV model, the Ambient Mean model, and the Ambient CV model, there is either nonconstant variance or non-normality of residuals. We will perform transformations of the response variable while keeping normality of the residuals under consideration.

## Model Fitting: Sun Mean Model

```{r}
m1 <- lmer(log(mean)~Month + Site + poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Sun"))

m1.5 <- lmer(log(mean)~Month + Site + poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Sun"))

vif(m1)
AIC(m1)
plot(m1)
qqnorm(resid(m1))

vif(m1.5)
AIC(m1.5)
plot(m1.5)
qqnorm(resid(m1.5))
```

This model looks suitable. However, the interpretation of the results will change: rather than saying going from one site to another is associated with an increase of x in the mean temperature, we would say it is associated with multiplying the mean by exp(x). This model also performs better in fit measurements (AIC) than the previous one, and has no multicollinearity issues. After comparing the model fit between the quadratic and the quartic time term, the quadratic appears to fit better, so it is fine to keep.

## Model Fitting: Sun CV Model

```{r}
m2 <- lmer(log(cv)~Month + Site + poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Sun"))

m2.5 <- lmer(log(cv)~Month + Site + poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Sun"))

AIC(m2)
vif(m2)
plot(m2)
qqnorm(resid(m2))

AIC(m2.5)
vif(m2.5)
plot(m2.5)
qqnorm(resid(m2.5))
```

This model looks suitable. However, the interpretation of the results will change: rather than saying going from one site to another is associated with an increase of x in the coefficient of variation of temperature, we would say it is associated with multiplying the coefficient of variation by exp(x). This model also performs better in fit measurements (lower AIC) than the previous one, and has no multicollinearity issues. It appears that in this case, the coefficient of variability is more accurately modeled using a quartic term than a quadratic term, based on the lower AIC.

## Model Fitting: Shade Mean Model

```{r}
m3 <- lmer(log(mean)~Month + Site + poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Shade"))

m3.5 <- lmer(log(mean)~Month + Site + poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Shade"))


vif(m3)
AIC(m3)
plot(m3)
qqnorm(resid(m3))

vif(m3.5)
AIC(m3.5)
plot(m3.5)
qqnorm(resid(m3.5))
```

This model looks suitable. However, the interpretation of the results will change: rather than saying going from one site to another is associated with an increase of x in the mean temperature, we would say it is associated with multiplying the mean by exp(x). This model also performs better in fit measurements (AIC) than the previous one, and has no multicollinearity issues. In this case, the quadratic term fits better than the quartic term.

## Model Fitting: Shade CV Model

```{r}
m4 <- lmer(log(cv)~Month + Site + poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Shade"))

m4.5 <- lmer(log(cv)~Month + Site + poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Shade"))

vif(m4)
AIC(m4)
plot(m4)
qqnorm(resid(m4))

vif(m4.5)
AIC(m4.5)
plot(m4.5)
qqnorm(resid(m4.5))
```

This model looks like it will either violate the constant variance assumption or normality of residuals. While a log transform fixes the constant variance assumption, it may induce non-normality of the residuals. However, this assumption is less sensitive to violation, so we would say proceed with caution. From what we understand, modeling the coefficient of variation may be of less importance than the mean. Regardless, the interpretation will be as previously mentioned. In this case, the gain in model fit from adding a quartic term is very minimal compared to the quadratic term and does not fix the non-normality of residuals.

## Model Fitting: Ambient Mean Model

```{r}
m5 <- lmer(log(mean)~Site + Month +poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Ambient",
                                      !Campus == "CSUSM"))

m5.5 <- lmer(log(mean)~Site + Month +poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Ambient",
                                      !Campus == "CSUSM"))

vif(m5)
AIC(m5)
plot(m5)
qqnorm(resid(m5))

vif(m5.5)
AIC(m5.5)
plot(m5.5)
qqnorm(resid(m5.5))
```

This model looks suitable after log transformation. This should be interpreted similar to the other mean models that were suitable. The quadratic term fits better than the quartic term, so we advise using that.

## Model Fitting: Ambient CV Model

```{r}
m6 <- lmer(log(cv)~Site + Month +poly(Time,2)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Ambient",
                                      !Campus == "CSUSM"))

m6.5 <- lmer(log(cv)~Site + Month +poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus), 
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Ambient",
                                      !Campus == "CSUSM"))

vif(m6)
AIC(m6)
plot(m6)
qqnorm(resid(m6))

vif(m6.5)
AIC(m6.5)
plot(m6.5)
qqnorm(resid(m6.5))
```

This model may violate assumptions with respect to normality of residuals, but once again, this assumption is less sensitive than other assumptions. This is likely fine to include. Once again, the quartic term gives very minimal gains compared to the quadratic term, so for parsimony we recommend sticking with the quadratic term.

## Checking model terms for each: site:month interaction?

```{r}
anova(m1)

intm1 <- lmer(log(mean)~Month*Site + poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus) + (1|Campus:Site) + (1|Campus:Site:Month),
                        data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer,
                                      Location == "Sun"))


anova(m1)
anova(intm1)

```

This is the final model that we recommend you to use. Please take note of which terms have an interaction and which are fixed vs. random effects.

### Predictions from Sun Mean Model

Here is code to make a comparison between on- and off-site temperatures for different months.

```{r}

####
# my chat prompt (Dr. Robinson)
# get the emmeans from this model over time for each site x month. then create a plot colored by site (on/off) and facet wrapped by month() using ggplot with time quantitative 
# 
# m1.5 <- lmer(log(mean) ~ Month*Site + poly(Time,4)+(1|Campus) + (1 | Site:Campus) + (1 | Month:Site:Campus), data = filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer, Location == "Sun"))
#   
# Use orange3 and steelblue as colors. also transform back to the original scale, not the log scale. 
# 
# ANDDDD use alpha blending for plotting the actual data under the predicted emmeans stuffs with 95% ci.. 
# 
# How good can you do at this?
######

library(emmeans)

# Create time grid for smooth predictions
time_grid <- with(
  filter(Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer, Location == "Sun"),
  seq(min(Time, na.rm = TRUE), max(Time, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 100)
)

# Estimated marginal means over quantitative Time,
# separately for Site x Month
emm_time <- emmeans(
  intm1,
  specs = ~ Site | Month * Time,
  at = list(Time = time_grid),
  type = "response"
)

emm_df <- as.data.frame(emm_time)

# Actual data on original scale
plot_dat <- Prelim_Stat_HourlyAvgs_lmer %>%
  filter(Location == "Sun")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = plot_dat,
    aes(x = Time, y = mean, color = Site, group = interaction(Site:Campus)),
    alpha = 0.18,
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = emm_df,
    aes(
      x = Time,
      ymin = asymp.LCL,
      ymax = asymp.UCL,
      fill = Site
    ),
    alpha = 0.22,
    color = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = emm_df,
    aes(x = Time, y = response, color = Site),
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Month) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Off" = "orange3", "On" = "steelblue")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Off" = "orange3", "On" = "steelblue")) +
  labs(
    x = "Time",
    y = "Mean Temperature",
    color = "Site",
    fill = "Site"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey90", color = NA)
  )
```

Since there is no interaction with time, the pairwise comparisons (difference) between on/off sites within each month is going to be the same at different times of the day. Here is an example of how to make comparisons for the on/off effect if the goal is to be month-specific.

```{r}
# Make comparisons within a given time
emmeans(
  intm1,
  specs = ~ Site | Month,
  at = list(Time = 10),
  type = "response"
) |>
  pairs()
```
